Yes and no. Lasers aren't "just light". Light is energy. Put enough energy into a focused spot and you will definitely do damage. Laser cutting machines can but through steel plates that are around an inch thick (with the right amount of power). Less powerful lasers can cut through wood and plastics. The problem though is the energy needs to be focused to a small spot to do the damage. A large and powerful beam would require a lot of setup to do damage at a distance and really isn't practical. Also, the amount of power needed to run a very high powered laser is not at all trivial. The materials involved can be highly troublesome and the losses of power over distance can make the whole thing impractical. Lasers are great for certain types of material damage, but laser weapons that have been on the drawing board for years don't have the economies of scale that industrial laser machines do. We're a long way from having practical and effective laser weapons, but the people of Voat will likely disagree with me based on what they think they know about the subject. The military hasn't switched to them (or rail guns for that matter) for a very good set of reasons. The tests have been okay, but they have too many drawbacks. The military prefers effective and reliable weapons and lasers are't there yet. Maybe someday...
Yeah but at what distance. I was assuming like a handgun or more distance. and what about EVERYTHING in between the target and the source?

That's the problem. Laser cutters use a very short focal length, usually a few inches or less. Because of the nature of the way light focuses through a lens or off a curved mirror, the light beam converges to a point at the focal length but then begins to spread out beyond the focal distance. The more the light spreads, the less energy it delivers to a surface. There's even more complicated issues in the beam energy in that the beam cross section has a Gaussian distribution (or multiple Gaussian distributions based on the laser's temporal mode) that make the outside edges of the beam far less powerful than the center(s) of the beam. Optics can't effectively utilize all the laser's beam energy in focusing so you get even more losses. Distance is a major impediment to the progress of light based weapons. A few feet of distance may as well be a few miles since the focal point is the only optimal spot where the laser an do damage. This is one of the many reasons I say we're not there yet and won't be for some time to come. And as for ANYTHING in the path to the target, yes that will totally fuck up the whole plan. Even the air in between will absorb a lot of the energy and cause more energy to scatter or distort. The physics of lasers is anything but simple.
